power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Improved understanding of how myelin damage contributes to disability in multiple sclerosis (MS) is needed to inform targeted therapeutic strategies and improve clinical trial platforms.

Magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) and T 1 relaxometry provide in vivo quantitative MRI measures of myelin integrity, and may offer insights into disability-relevant pathology beyond inflammatory relapse.

This longitudinal study explores the relationship between early demyelination and disability progression over the first five years following diagnosis. 62 people with relapsing-remitting (pwRR)MS (≤ 6 months post-diagnosis, 48 female, mean age 38 years) underwent baseline and one-year MRI and Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) assessment.
At five-year follow-up, 56/62 (90.3%) completed EDSS and 40/62 additionally completed MRI (64.5%).
Disability progression was defined as an increase of ≥ 1.5, ≥ 1.0 or ≥ 0.5 points for a previous EDSS score of < 1.0, 1.0 to 5.5, and ≥ 6.0, respectively.
text.formatted: Disability progression was defined as an increase of ≥ 1.5, ≥ 1.0 or ≥ 0.5 points for a previous EDSS score of < 1.0, 1.0 to 5.5, and ≥ 6.0, respectively.

text.text: Baseline neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and EBNA1 immunoglobulin (IgG) titres were also measured.
MTsat was calculated within normal-appearing white matter (NAWM), white matter lesions (WML), cortical and deep grey matter (GM) structures.
Associations between change in MTsat and disability progression were assessed with binomial logistic regression.
Interactions with interval disease activity (i.e. new/enlarging lesions [NELs]) were investigated, and comparisons were made with healthy control test-retest data (n = 11).

Exploratory analyses were performed for: (prolonged) T 1 ; baseline metrics; blood-derived markers; diffusion-weighted imaging; and, disability-associated differences in five-year microstructural MRI trajectories.

Greater baseline-to-one-year decreases in NAWM and WML MTsat were associated with baseline-to-one-year disability progression (adjusted odds ratio [95% confidence interval] = 0.255 [0.078 to 0.602] and 0.261 [0.084 to 0.638]; false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected p-.

Immune-mediated demyelination in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) is thought to result in axonal damage, leading to neuronal dysfunction and clinical disability. 1, 2 Modulation of neuroinflammatory pathways with current disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) reduces rates of clinical relapse and new or enlarging white matter lesions (NELs), and slows disability progression. 3 It is increasingly recognised however that disability accumulation in RRMS may also occur independently of DMT-modifiable inflammatory relapse activity, termed 'silent progression' or progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA). 4 The pathological processes underlying disability progression in early RRMS and the variable trajectories of evolving disability for individual patients, however, remain poorly understood.

text.formatted: Diffuse myelin and axonal damage within normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) and grey matter (NAGM) are known pathological features of RRMS, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> and microstructural MRI allows more specific non-invasive quantification of myelin and axonal integrity than is possible with conventional structural imaging. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> Magnetization transfer imaging (MTI) detects signal indirectly from protons bound to macromolecules, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> which are not distinguishable on conventional MRI sequences.

text.text: In healthy white matter (WM), this signal is dominated by myelin-bound protons, hence providing a degree of specificity for quantifying myelin content.

The magnetization transfer ratio (MTR) has been extensively applied to the study of MS, although reported relationships between MTR and disability have varied. 16 A recent meta-analysis which included RRMS cohorts of varying disease duration showed a negative association between NAWM MTR and Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores, 16 however many individual studies found no such relationship. [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] [24] [25] The smaller number of analyses of NAGM MTR in mixed disease duration cohorts showed no significant association with EDSS. 16 MTR data are confounded by T 1 relaxation and B 1 + magnetic field inhomogeneity effects, which may result in both increased variance and systematic bias in myelin estimation, and may partially account for inconsistent findings across different studies.

text.text: To date, MTsat has seen limited application in MS (Supplementary Table 1),  although one cross-sectional study has reported associations between clinical disability and NAWM MTsat, but not MTR. 34 The variable flip angle (VFA) T 1 approximation required for MTsat calculation provides an additional quantitative measure of T 1 , which is also thought to be a proxy for myelin density. 48 More marked focal T 1 prolongation within WML provides a quantitative correlate of visible T 1 -weighted 'black hole' lesions, which are known to be associated with MS disease progression. 49 The relationships between changes in myelin integrity in visible lesions and normal-appearing brain, measured using MTsat, disability progression, and interactions with radiological interval disease activity remain unexplored in early RRMS.

text.text: The primary aims of this study are to determine the degree to which demyelination, measured longitudinally in vivo using MTsat in NAWM and WML, (a) drives clinical disability progression in the five years following diagnosis of RRMS, (b) predicts future disability progression, and c) how the relationship between myelin integrity and disability relates to interval inflammatory disease activity reflected in NELs.

As exploratory aims, we explore the association between early T 1 changes and disability progression over five years in this early RRMS cohort, and re-examine previous analyses of disability evolution over one year using more stringent and widely-used definitions of disability worsening.

We additionally examine associations between baseline myelin measures, diffusion-weighted imaging (dMRI)-derived metrics, blood-derived markers of neuroaxonal damage and disability progression, and we explore whether and how trajectories of five-year microstructural changes co-vary with disability progression.

text.text: MRI data included: (1) a 3D T 1 -weighted Magnetization Prepared Rapid Acquisition Gradient Echo (MPRAGE) and (2) 2D dual echo (DE) for brain tissue segmentation; (3) 2D fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) for WML segmentation; (4) two 3D proton density fast low-angle shot spoiled gradient echo (SPGR) images with and without a Gaussian saturation pulse (9.984 ms; 500°) at 1.2 kHz offset from the water frequency, plus an additional 3D SPGR T 1 -weighted image required for MTsat and VFA T 1 calculation; and, (4) multi-shell 2D diffusion-weighted spin-echo echoplanar imaging (151 directions; 0/200/500/1000/2000 s/mm2 b-values) with an additional three reverse phase-encoding volumes (b=0 s/mm2) to derive diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) parameters.
Full MRI acquisition parameters are given in Supplementary Table 2.

text.text: Primary analyses examined the association between change in regional MTsat between time points, and disability progression between the same and future time points was assessed with binomial logistic regression, adjusted for baseline age, sex, change in WML volume, baseline MTsat, and dichotomised DMT usage.

The majority of participants were treated with lowefficacy DMTs or untreated at one-year (93.5%) and five-years (80.3%); there was thus limited scope to further interrogate the effect of high-efficacy treatment on associations.
False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction was performed.

Overall goodness-of-fit was assessed with Nagelkerke's 64 (pseudo)-R² (rms package). 65 Log-Likelihood Ratios with Wald's chisquared (χ 2 ) tests and, when significant, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) were used to compare models against the null model and the reference model, i.e. with microstructural MRI markers removed. 66, 67 Odds ratios were calculated for coefficients of z-normalised variables.

text.text: To determine the robustness of findings, analyses were repeated excluding the five observations with the largest Cook's distance per model.

For significant primary models, to determine the influence of interval disease activity, models were repeated with inclusion of an interaction term between change over time in the given metric and NEL group.
Analyses were repeated for T 1 , prolonged T 1 voxel count in WML, NODDI, DTI, and baseline microstructural metrics to determine associations with disability progression.
Baseline models included baseline WML volume, age and sex as covariates.
As NfL and GFAP are markers of neuroaxonal damage, and EBNA1 titres are elevated in people with MS, blood-derived markers were also added to primary analyses to determine incremental value.

To determine retrospectively whether the trajectory of microstructural changes differed between those who did or did not experience disability progression in the five years following diagnosis, participants with complete MRI and EDSS data were split into disability groups: 'progressors' who experienced disability progression between baseline and one-year, and between one-year and five-years; 'early progressors' who only showed progression between baseline and one-year; 'late progressors' who only progressed between one-year and fiveyears; and, 'non-progressors' with no evidence of progression between time points.

Linear mixed-effects models, with baseline age, sex, baseline WML load, and DMT usage as covariates, were used to determine whether the microstructural metric significantly depends on the interaction term between progression group and time.

text.text: In this study, we investigate associations between quantitative microstructural MRI markers of myelin integrity and disability progression in the five years following RRMS diagnosis.
We show that longitudinal groupwise one-year change in NAWM MTsat is associated with contemporaneous disability progression, but does not predict the subsequent four years of disability progression.
We also demonstrate a relationship between decreasing MTsat in WML and disability progression over the first year, but not over subsequent one-to-five-year follow-up.

We find no evidence to suggest that disability progression associated with early NAWM or WML demyelination is influenced by the presence of NELs, suggesting that changes in myelin integrity may occur independently of radiological inflammatory disease activity in recently diagnosed RRMS.

We also find evidence of progressive demyelination within GM and the majority of deep GM structures, which is detectable with MTsat, but generally show only modest associations with early disability progression.

Exploratory analyses show that the trajectory of WML MTsat nominally differs between individuals with different five-year disability progression trajectories; however, this finding does not survive FDR correction.
Neither T 1 nor any baseline metrics are associated with disability progression, and blood-derived NfL, GFAP and EBNA-1 markers did not provide incremental value to models.

Diffuse NAWM abnormalities in pwMS, detected with quantitative MR techniques including MTR are well-documented; 68 insights into the pathological drivers of disability divergence in early MS have, however, been limited by technique sensitivity and specificity.

text.text: MTsat is thought to be more specific to myelin than MTR due to inherent correction for T 1 relaxation effects (and, to some degree, B 1 + inhomogeneities), 26 and is strongly associated with myelin marker Luxol-Fast Blue. 69 We previously observed a groupwise longitudinal decrease in MTsat in NAWM in our cohort of newly diagnosed pwRRMS, suggestive of widespread progressive demyelination. 37 Here, we report for the first time that greater decreases in MTsat in NAWM in the year following RRMS diagnosis are associated with a significantly increased likelihood of early disability progression over the same one-year period.
text.formatted: MTsat is thought to be more specific to myelin than MTR due to inherent correction for T 1 relaxation effects (and, to some degree, B 1 + inhomogeneities), <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26</ref> and is strongly associated with myelin marker Luxol-Fast Blue. <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">69</ref> We previously observed a groupwise longitudinal decrease in MTsat in NAWM in our cohort of newly diagnosed pwRRMS, suggestive of widespread progressive demyelination. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">37</ref> Here, we report for the first time that greater decreases in MTsat in NAWM in the year following RRMS diagnosis are associated with a significantly increased likelihood of early disability progression over the same one-year period.

text.text: Our findings suggest that early subtle demyelination beyond visible WML contributes significantly to worsening disability.

The absence of any significant interaction between change in NAWM MTsat and NELs on disability evolution suggests that progressive 'invisible' myelin loss (demyelination and/or failure of remyelination) may be one of the substrates underlying progression in early RRMS, and occurs independently of MRI-visible inflammation.
This may provide a potential mechanism underlying PIRA, 70 and may have important treatment implications.
text.formatted: This may provide a potential mechanism underlying PIRA, <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">70</ref> and may have important treatment implications.

text.text: The sample size of the current study, however, limits further robust interrogation of PIRA and relapseassociated worsening (RAW) phenotypes beyond the presence of NELs.

Our findings broadly support the hypothesis that disability in early MS is predominantly driven by a diffuse 'smouldering' pathological process, rather than by episodic focal inflammatory episodes. 71 While paramagnetic rims around WML are thought to be a localised manifestation of chronic inflammation, 72 widespread NAWM microglial activation, detected with PET and associated with microstructural disruption and disability, has also been reported in a mixed MS subtype cohort. 73 It is not yet clear whether the widespread disability-relevant myelin loss demonstrated here results directly from more global brain inflammation in early RRMS.

text.text: Although one-year change in NAWM MTsat was associated with one-year disability progression, it was not predictive of one-to-five-year disability progression.
One-to-five-year change in NAWM MTsat was also not associated with disability progression over that same period.
There are a number of possible explanations for this.
The rate of disability-relevant myelin loss may vary with time in MS.
Indeed, we observed that the annualised MTsat change over the first year was more pronounced than over the subsequent four years.
Trajectory over the first year following diagnosis is therefore not necessarily a predictor of disease behaviour over subsequent years.

Variation in the efficacy of repair mechanisms in NAWM and treatment with DMTs during the one-to-five-year period may also mitigate longer term disability progression, and weaken any predictive relationship.

Change in MTsat over five years is modest, and larger subject numbers or measurement over a longer period may be needed to identify statistically significant associations with and predictors of disability during this disease phase.

Here, we demonstrate an association between changes in WML MTsat and disability progression over one year, although that change is not predictive of forward disability progression from one to five years.

Within our recently diagnosed RRMS cohort, we previously noted a net increase in WML MTsat over time, 37 which we speculated could be caused either by spontaneous remyelination after an acute inflammatory episode that prompted diagnosis, or reduction in oedema following acute inflammation in lesions; this accords with other evidence that remyelination within lesions may occur to a varying extent across patients. 74 When grouped by EDSS progression trajectory however, we observe in this study that participants in our recently-diagnosed RRMS cohort with progression between time points tended to demonstrate a decrease in MTsat within WML, whilst an increase in WML MTsat was more commonly observed in those without progression.

text.text: This suggests that recruitment of innate myelin repair mechanisms within focal WML may slow progression.

Myelin-sensitive MTR within lesions has previously been applied as an endpoint in a remyelinating therapy trial, 75 and MTsat may provide a more sensitive and specific end point for such studies in future.
text.formatted: Myelin-sensitive MTR within lesions has previously been applied as an endpoint in a remyelinating therapy trial, <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">75</ref> and MTsat may provide a more sensitive and specific end point for such studies in future.

text.text: The observation that MTsat changes in WML over a year do not predict one-to-five-year disability progression suggests that early spontaneous remyelination of already-extensivelydamaged tissue does little to mitigate long-term disability accrual.
The absence of detectable association with future disability progression could additionally be explained by technical MTsat 'floor effects' due to already very low myelin density within some WML.

Previous studies have suggested that GM damage may contribute disproportionately to early disability progression in MS, [76] [77] [78] and cortical MTR changes indicative of myelin loss and repair measured over a year in a mixed MS cohort have recently been shown to predict disability after a five-year interval. 78 In our early MS cohort, we found that cortical GM myelin changes measured with MTsat were significantly associated with one-year disability progression, which accords with previous findings.

text.text: This model was, however, no better than the null (intercept-only) model, suggesting that GM may be marginally influential, but not the primary disability driver in the model.

As with NAWM and WML, one-year cortical myelin change also did not predict one-to-five year disability progression and one-to-five year myelin changes were not associated with disability progression over the same period.
Cortical GM is more sparsely myelinated than WM; low myelin density may reduce the accuracy of our myelin-sensitive metrics within the cortex.
Poor detection of cortical GM lesions at 3 T clinical field strengths precludes reliable segmentation and therefore microstructural characterisation of focal cortical lesions.

Our findings overall indicate that disability-relevant myelin changes occur within the cortex in early RRMS, but are difficult to detect without specific myelin-sensitized acquisition techniques, and may not predict longer term disability outcomes.

We observed a relationship between combined deep GM change in MTsat and one-year disability progression, in addition to individual associations with MTsat changes in the thalamus, basal ganglia and hippocampus.

Histopathology has demonstrated demyelination in deep GM in MS. 79 We are not aware of any study examining associations between longitudinal myelin changes within deep GM using MTsat and disability progression in recently-diagnosed RRMS.
text.formatted: Histopathology has demonstrated demyelination in deep GM in MS. <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">79</ref> We are not aware of any study examining associations between longitudinal myelin changes within deep GM using MTsat and disability progression in recently-diagnosed RRMS.

text.text: Our results illustrate that deep GM demyelination occurs at an early stage of disease and contributes to disability progression, albeit to a lesser extent than NAWM demyelination.

Although the thalamus is often classified as a GM structure, it is has complex internal anatomy and contains significant myelinated WM. 80 A recent study showed no difference in two-year change in thalamic MTsat-derived myelin volume fraction (MVF) between healthy controls and pwRRMS of mixed disease duration. 42 Previous work in early RRMS found that thalamic MTR was negatively associated with timepoint-averaged EDSS; the rate of MTR change was not associated with EDSS at two-year follow-up however. 81 In later disease, reduced thalamic myelin density compared with healthy controls has been observed with MTR, 82, 83 and inhomogeneous (ih)MTR. 83 Our finding of a relationship between thalamic MTsat and disability progression over one year, but not five years, broadly accords with these findings.

text.text: Although myelin loss within the thalamus appears relevant to early disability progression, our results do not support the view that early thalamic demyelination predicts sustained disability progression over a longer time period.
In the basal ganglia, which comprise the caudate, putamen and pallidum, greater demyelination was associated with one-year disability progression in our early RRMS cohort.

We are not aware of any other studies examining disability progression and demyelination measured with MTsat within the basal ganglia, although some evidence supports crosssectional associations between disability and myelin proton fraction (MPF) within the caudate nucleus and putamen in MS. 84 Basal ganglia demyelination however did not differentiate between those who did and did not progress at five-year follow-up, and is therefore not a stratifier of future disease trajectory.

text.text: Decreasing MTsat in the hippocampus appeared to significantly increase the likelihood of disability progression at one year in our newly-diagnosed RRMS cohort.

Hippocampal demyelination is a known histopathological feature of MS, 85 and significant associations between EDSS and myelin-sensitive χ-separation quantitative susceptibility dependent MRI of the hippocampi have been reported. 86 Lower hippocampal sub-field volumes have also been reported in early RRMS compared with healthy controls 87 and with MS diagnosis in people with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS). 88 There are, however, a number of confounds that may contribute to our findings.
text.formatted: Hippocampal demyelination is a known histopathological feature of MS, <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">85</ref> and significant associations between EDSS and myelin-sensitive χ-separation quantitative susceptibility dependent MRI of the hippocampi have been reported. <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">86</ref> Lower hippocampal sub-field volumes have also been reported in early RRMS compared with healthy controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">87</ref> and with MS diagnosis in people with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS). <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">88</ref> There are, however, a number of confounds that may contribute to our findings.

text.text: The morphology of the hippocampus and adjacent CSF and choroid plexus in the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle make reliable segmentation difficult, and a small number of contributing voxels and partial volume effects from adjacent structures make MTsat signal vulnerable to subtle volume change.
Moreover, susceptibility effects from the sphenoid bone and sinus may also influence signal return.

The hippocampus primarily subserves memory function, and mechanisms underlying any direct causal relationship between hippocampal dysfunction and EDSS which is substantially motorweighted should also be considered.

Cognitive testing of specific memory domains is needed to elucidate any relationship between early hippocampal demyelination and progression of memory deficits, which appear more prevalent in MS with longer disease duration. 89 Although our findings suggest possible disability-relevant hippocampal changes in RRMS, we therefore interpret these with caution.

text.text: We found no significant association between baseline MTsat and subsequent disability progression.

This accords with previous cross-sectional studies which found no association between myelin measures and EDSS; 28, 30, 32 although those studies examined EDSS at a single time point rather than change over time.
text.formatted: This accords with previous cross-sectional studies which found no association between myelin measures and EDSS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">32</ref> although those studies examined EDSS at a single time point rather than change over time.

text.text: Our data from a sizeable cohort of recently diagnosed pwRRMS support the view that a single time point MRI measure of microstructural integrity is insufficient to predict EDSS clinical disability evolution over one year or five years.
It is, however, possible that such associations may become apparent with longer follow-up, or with the development of more nuanced disability measures.
In contrast to MTsat, we found no evidence of associations between disability and NAWM T 1, nor of prolonged T 1 WML voxels and disability progression in our exploratory analyses.

While we have previously reported a relationship between NAWM T 1 and prolonged T 1 WML and EDSS disability progression in our cohort using a ≥ 0.5 point threshold, 50 here we show that, unlike associations with MTsat, this relationship does not persist with more stringent clinical criteria.
text.formatted: While we have previously reported a relationship between NAWM T 1 and prolonged T 1 WML and EDSS disability progression in our cohort using a ≥ 0.5 point threshold, <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">50</ref> here we show that, unlike associations with MTsat, this relationship does not persist with more stringent clinical criteria.

text.text: We also previously reported relationships between longitudinal T 1 measures in deep GM and one-year disability progression; 50 again, these are not seen with more stringent progression criteria or as predictors of five-year disability worsening.

Floor effects have been observed previously with T 1 prolongation in lesions, 48 which may contribute to our null findings, and T 1 changes in sparsely-myelinated cortex are likely to be dominated by factors other than myelin density.

text.text: We have previously reported longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) or Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging 60 findings over one year in this cohort, 37 and note that we also found no significant relationships between disability progression and any diffusion metrics for any brain region (Supplementary Material 2).

text.text: Our current results suggest that MTsat is a more sensitive measure than T 1 for detecting subtle diffuse demyelination that causes more pronounced and longer-term disability progression.
MTsat may therefore be more appropriate as a clinical trial surrogate endpoint, using widely accepted definitions of disability progression.

The FutureMS study was designed to recruit a cohort at a homogeneous disease stage; variation in recruitment with regard to the time of first reported symptom onset was not explicitly included in our analyses due to the poor reliability of determining first symptom onset compared with date of diagnosis, and a strong association with age.

We also did not account for possible bias introduced by exclusion of subjects at recruitment, nor due to missing data; it is difficult to establish in which direction this may have biased our conclusions.

We acknowledge the limitations of the EDSS as a measure of disability, including the noncontinuous and non-normal distribution of scores within MS cohorts. 67 More nuanced, longitudinal cognitive testing, particularly with respect to memory deficits , may be required to fully elucidate the contribution of deep GM demyelination to disability progression.

text.text: All participants were treatment-naïve at baseline, and dichotomised use of DMTs between time points was included as a covariate in our models.

FutureMS is, however, a 'real world' observational cohort and participants may initiate or switch DMTs between time points for a variety of reasons (including interval disease activity, risk profiles and adverse effects).
B 1 + correction was not performed; MTsat, however, inherently corrects B 1 + inhomogeneities to some degree.

Although longitudinal measurements will mitigate the impact of residual B 1 + inhomogeneities, and the occurrence of a systematic difference in B 1 + distribution between disability groups is unlikely, the accuracy of cross-sectional T 1 , and to a certain extent MTsat, may be reduced.
Our future studies will include acquisition of B 1 + maps.
Lesion filling prior to brain tissue segmentation was not performed.
Comparisons between segmentations performed with and without lesion filling (data not shown) demonstrate the impact on resulting brain tissue masks is minimal-to-none.
Understanding technique reproducibility is important for establishing sensitivity to longitudinal biological change.

While changes in MTsat over one year were significant at the group level, test-retest limits of agreement established in healthy control WM indicate that they will not necessarily distinguish between individuals with stable/improving and those with worsening disability (see Supplementary Results).
Moreover, technique reproducibility measured in healthy control data over a two-week period may underestimate test-retest variability over the one-year interval studied here in pwRRMS.
Conclusion imaging is associated with one-year disability progression in early RRMS, independently of interval radiological disease activity.
text.formatted: <head>Conclusion</head> imaging is associated with one-year disability progression in early RRMS, independently of interval radiological disease activity.

text.text: Widespread ongoing disability-relevant demyelination in WML and GM is also seen over the year following MS diagnosis.
None of our microstructural measures predict future disability progression, and indeed myelin changes over the subsequent four years were modest and not associated with disability progression.

Our findings provide potential mechanisms driving early disability progression beyond NELs, and suggest that microstructural evaluation of NAWM (and perhaps GM) may be at least as important as WML features for assessing disease trajectory.
Quantitative myelin measures therefore provide an important adjunct to conventional indicators of activity for assessing otherwise 'hidden' disease evolution and therapeutic response in RRMS.
Greater myelin changes over the first year but not subsequently suggest a disease tempo change and point towards a potentially important window of therapeutic opportunity.

MTsat shows promise as a clinically-applicable disease stratifier and surrogate endpoint in future therapeutic trials, especially those targeted at preventing progression in those without radiological inflammatory disease activity.
